newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-BOLIVIA AND ARGENTINA SWAP ACCUSATIONS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BOLIVIA AND ARGENTINA SWAP ACCUSATIONS.

text.p: Bolivia and Argentina on Thursday blamed each other for the brawl which interrupted their World Cup qualifier for 10 minutes on Wednesday.
A similar incident marred Paraguay's 2-1 win over Colombia in Asuncion.
Argentina's press reacted with horror and indignation to the clash on Wednesday which left their team physically bruised and in danger of missing the 1998 World Cup finals in France.

The Argentine media claimed the battle began when striker Julio Cruz was attacked trying to collect the match ball near the Bolivian team bench. They said Cruz was knocked to the ground by a player on the bench.
Other Argentine players then attempted to exact revenge, at which point local police intervened.

One Argentine television network showed film of what it claimed to be a local policeman spraying a substance in the face of reserve goalkeeper German Roja. They accused Bolivian fans of throwing objects at the Argentine players.
"Argentina played badly and the police played dirty," said Clarin. La Prensa said Cruz had suffered a brutal attack and described the scenes at the end as resembling a "horror film."

But several newspapers also condemned the attitude of the Argentine players. They were also highly critical of the performance which led to the 2-1 defeat and left Argentina fifth in the group, behind Bolivia and Ecuador.
"The worst thing Argentina can do is pose as the only victim," said La Nacion. "Argentina proposed the fight but the Bolivians accepted the ridiculous invitation to take it to a higher level."

Clarin wrote: "The cowardly attack on the physiotherapist Hernan Arsenian, the treacherous punch thrown at Julio Cruz, the paralyzing gas that knocked out Roja, these attacks ... cannot wipe out the shame caused by the unintelligent attitude of the Argentine players."

La Nacion wrote that the Argentina team turned to violence when they realized they were losing despite three weeks of altitude training in the Andes to prepare for the match in La Paz, at 14,000 feet (3,600 metres) above sea level.
Brazilian referee Sidrack Marinho, who sent off two Argentine players, was universally condemned in Argentina and widely praised in his own country.

Bolivians put the blame on Argentina's players for causing a series of incidents during the game. They were incensed when Gustava Zapata, sent off in the second half, then started a fight with Demetrio Angola as he left the pitch.
"The Argentines resorted to punching and hitting when they were beaten," said Hoy, a daily newspaper. "The Bolivian bench rose to the provocation."
Two Argentines were sent off during the match before the first all-out fight, which broke out after Zapata refused the referee's order to leave the pitch.
But the biggest brawl began near the end when Cruz ran off the pitch to fetch the ball near the Bolivian bench.
After Cruz was punched several times, other Argentine players and Bolivian riot police joined in the fight whilst spectators hurled projectiles at everybody.
"They beat us at soccer and at boxing too," lamented one fan in Buenos Aires.

Argentina's much-criticized coach Daniel Passarella said he would complain to the South American Football Confederation. Clarin speculated that Argentina might argue it should get the three points for victory instead of Bolivia.
But two times world champions Argentina, trailing fifth in the South American qualifying group, need to improve if they are to make it to France.

In the Paraguay-Colombia match, players, both team benches and police became embroiled in battle after the sendings-off of Paraguayan goalkeeper Jose Luis Chilavert and Colombian striker Faustino Asprilla in the second half.

The two clashed in the Paraguayan penalty area in an incident from which Colombia were awarded a penalty. The Paraguayans maintained the fiery Chilavert was innocent, having been punched by Asprilla after a verbal exchange.
"I don't know why I was sent off. I said absolutely nothing to Asprilla," said Chilavert. "We are not friends on the field .... I don't want to be his friend off it either."
Asprilla said only: "The referee saw everything that happened."
The Colombian media were more worried about what they saw as the team's poor performance, singling out captain Carlos Valderrama and goalkeeper Farid Mondragon for the harshest criticism.
"All that scandal for nothing," said El Tiempo.
